scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The Near East Foundation Special Collections contains the personal papers of individuals associated with the Near East Foundation, including Laurence H. and Frances C. MacDaniels, Caleb Wakefield Lawrence, and Carl Birky and Pauline Birky-Kreutzer. The files include correspondence written during the American Committee for Relief in the Near East, Near East Relief, and Near East Foundation periods, a summary of NEF history, various publications, and slides taken by Carl Birky in Iran in the mid-1950s.

did.unittitle: Laurence H. and Frances C. MacDaniels papers

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Laurence Howland MacDaniels and Frances Cochran MacDaniels served in the American Committee for Near East Relief (later Near East Relief) for one year of service leaving for Brest, France on the USS Leviathan on February 16, 1919, and returned to the United States on July 14, 1920. Laurence MacDaniels served as General Manager and Assistant Director of the Harpoot Unit and Frances was cashier and bookkeeper of the Harpoot Unit and served the orphanage there.

The MacDaniels were graduates of Oberlin College in 1912. Laurence McDaniel received a Ph.D. from Cornell in 1917, serving as an instructor in botany from 1914 to 1917. When he returned to Cornell in the fall of 1920, he was an assistant professor of pomology and in 1923 was promoted to professor. In 1940, MacDaniels was appointed head of the Department of Floriculture and Ornamental Horticulture, a position he held until his retirement in 1956. While on leave from Cornell from 1943-1945, he served in the Bekaa Valley of Lebanon as director of agricultural extension for the Near East Foundation.
Laurence H. MacDaniels and Frances C. MacDaniels died in 1986.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The MacDaniels papers consist of letters written by the MacDaniels during their service in the American Committee for Relief in the Near East (ACRNE) and Near East Relief (NER) as well as documents related to their service. The letters include the MacDaniels' ACRNE appointment letters, copies of cables sent to families, letters from: New York City, aboard the Leviathan, Brest, Marseilles, aboard Gloucester Castle, Salonika, Constantinople, Derinje, Harpoot, Behisny, Malatia, Sivas, Cairo, and Athens. There are postcards, copies of letters from the Department of State, letters describing daily life in Turkey, the October 1919 News Bulletin published by the Near East Relief, correspondence with Henry Riggs, and commendation letters. There are also clippings and envelopes. A letter from June 29, 1919, describes the Harpoot Orphanage..

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The Caleb Wakefield Lawrence papers consist of correspondence from 1918-1924 pertaining to his role as a field secretary with the YMCA in France in 1918 and his role in relief work in Turkey. In 1919, following the war, Caleb Wakefield Lawrence and his wife Helen Lewis Lawrence became missionaries with the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions and returned to Smryna, where they lived prior to World War I. He resumed his work as a professor at the International College. His correspondents include James L. Barton, Harold Jaquith, and C. Claflin Davis. Lawrence served as Chairman of the Smyrna Disaster Relief Committee of the Constantinople Chapter of the American Red Cross.

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Caleb Wakefield Lawrence was born in 1868 in Maine and later lived in Boston. In 1896, he became an American Board missionary teacher and went to Smyrna, Turkey where his sister worked as a teacher. For three years he tutored at the Boys' School, which later became the International College. He met his future wife, Helen Lewis, a teacher at the missionary school in 1897.

Helen studied nursing in London, and Caleb completed distance courses from Queen's University, Kingston, Ontario, Canada, and graduated with a degree in History and Literature. Helen and Caleb were married in 1904 and had seven children together. Caleb became a professor at the International College in Smyrna.

The family left Turkey prior to World War I, and Caleb served as a field secretary with the YMCA in France in 1918. In 1919, following the war, Caleb and Helen became missionaries with the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions and returned to Smyrna, where they lived prior to World War I. Caleb resumed his work as a professor at the International College. Beginning on September 6, 1922, until June 30, 1923, Caleb served as Chairman of the Disaster Relief Committee of Smyrna of the Constantinople Chapter of the American Red Cross. Caleb retired from teaching in 1933. The family moved to Norton, Massachusetts, and Caleb died in 1939. Helen died in 1963.

did.unittitle: Carl Birky and Pauline Birky-Kreutzer papers

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Pauline Livengood was born in 1916 in Atwood, Illinois. Carl Birky was born in 1903 in Champaign, Illinois. Pauline and Carl married on July 26, 1936. They lived in Urbana, Illinois while Carl pursued graduate studies at the University of Illinois, and Pauline worked for the Farm Security Administration, becoming a District Supervisor.
In 1945, Carl accepted a faculty position at Indiana University. In 1948, they moved with their son and daughter to Fort Collins, Colorado where Carl became a professor at Colorado State University.

In 1956, Pauline and Carl moved to Tehran, Iran, for two years where they worked as advisors in the community development program of the Near East Foundation. Upon their return to Fort Collins, Pauline became a Research Associate at Colorado State University.

In 1960, Pauline participated in a congressional feasibility study that led to the founding of the Peace Corps under President John F. Kennedy. Pauline directed Peace Corps training programs for West Pakistan and Afghanistan. She worked in Lahore, West Pakistan, from 1962-1963, where she led the Peace Corps program.
Pauline served as director of the Center for Research and Education (CRE) from 1962 until 1975, when she retired. Carl died in 1976.
In 1978, Pauline married William Kreutzer. She married Richard Kreutzer in 1998.
In 2003, Pauline wrote and published "Peace Corps Pioneer," an autobiographical account of her experiences in Iran and Pakistan.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The Carl Birky and Pauline Birky-Kreutzer papers consist primarily of slides taken by Carl in Iran from 1956-1958. There are also contract documents and reports from their time with the Near East Foundation, pamphlets relating to Iran and NEF, copies of the Tehran Journal, and Pauline Birky-Kreutzer's 2003 memoir, Peace Corps Pioneer or "The Perils of Pauline."
